title: Mannheim water capacity risk framework approved
subtitle: Wilmot water transfer safeguards, deferred 10% resiliency target, servicing transfers, conservation and independent capital plan review.
overview: Regional Council held a special meeting on the water capacity constraint in the Mannheim Service Area, which has stalled new development approvals. After hearing many delegations, Council adopted staff's Scenario 2 interim risk management framework {{vote:m8}}. The framework defers planned shutdowns of water facilities until sidestream treatment at the Mannheim plant is in service and phases in the resiliency target.

Council also approved an interim extra 15 L/s from the Wilmot Centre well supply, with safeguards for Wilmot residents. These include emergency water help beyond the historic well interference area {{vote:m14}}. Council asked for a report on transferring existing allocations within unbuilt developments by July 8 {{vote:m3}}.

A proposed 10% resiliency target was not decided. It will return on June 17 after the provincial land facilitation office reviews it {{vote:m9}}. Council also asked for a forward-looking servicing policy, more conservation work and an independent peer review of the capital plan. For residents and builders, new allocations remain limited until more capacity comes online.

decisions.detail: Council adopted Scenario 2, deferring planned shutdowns of water supply facilities until Mannheim sidestream treatment is fully in service and phasing in the operational resiliency target.

Council allocated an additional 15 L/s from the Wilmot Centre well supply as a temporary bridge, ending when sidestream capacity is operational, with emergency water help and a burden of proof on the Region for Wilmot well interference claims until a new policy is adopted.
Council set the question of a 10% maximum initial resiliency target to be considered on June 17, 2026, with the provincial land facilitation office asked to review and advise.
Staff must report by July 8, 2026 on a framework for transferring existing water servicing allocations within an unbuilt development where reserve capacity exists.
Staff must report by June 17, 2026 on a forward-looking servicing policy, in consultation with area municipalities and the provincial development facilitator's office.
Council deferred to June 17, 2026 the request to provide clarity and sign off on Form 1s so fully approved projects can proceed with conditional building permits and phased construction.
Council directed the Region to enable and prioritize water conservation work with the residential development and ICI sectors while working toward a 20% longer-term resiliency factor.
Council directed engagement of the Ontario Clean Water Agency to peer review the Region's capital plan and support its delivery for three to five years, accelerating delayed projects.

debate: Development-industry delegates argued the framework was too restrictive. They asked for a 10% interim resiliency target, conditional permits and phased construction, and said six months of delays have frozen projects, investment and jobs.

Staff said a fixed or capped percentage would undermine the framework, which uses a fluid target tied to emergencies and critical maintenance. They said it would lengthen the period in which Form 1s cannot be signed because the system is in a supply deficit.

An outside water-industry expert told Council that decision-makers carry personal and legal liability for drinking water safety under the Safe Drinking Water Act. The chair's decision to let this expert speak was challenged and upheld {{vote:m7}}.

Wilmot residents, a fish hatchery and groundwater advocates raised concerns about falling water levels and private wells. They asked for transparency, a hydrogeological review and compensation. Staff said emergency water help outside the historic compensation area was too broad. The Wilmot councillor said more pumping could affect residents beyond that area.
On the capital plan review, one councillor called it experts checking experts. Others said an independent Ontario Clean Water Agency review would help rebuild public trust.
